questions.q: How does the lesson describe the relationship between red-teaming and Chapter 1's risk categories?
options: Red-teaming replaces the need to understand those risk categories at all
Red-teaming turns those categories from theoretical concepts into a repeatable, measured test suite run against your own application
Red-teaming only applies to risks not covered in Chapter 1
Red-teaming is unrelated to any of the Chapter 1 risk categories
questions.explain: The lesson frames red-teaming as where Chapter 1's risk categories stop being theoretical and become a repeatable, measured test suite.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a red-team tool needs context about the application, not just the model?
options: Because the model's name is irrelevant to any testing
Because specific context about what the app does and what it can reach drives more realistic generated attacks
Because red-team tools cannot function without a company logo
Because applications never have any data worth protecting
questions.explain: The lesson explains that the more specific the application description, the more realistic the generated attacks will be.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does a real red-team run typically look like at scale?
options: A single manual conversation with the model
Thousands of generated probes across many attack categories, executed automatically
One test case reviewed by a committee
A one-time email sent to the AI vendor
questions.explain: The lesson describes a real run as generating and executing thousands of probes across many categories, not a handful of manual tries.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say critical and high-severity findings should come first, regardless of the overall pass rate?
options: Because overall pass rate is always more important than any individual finding
Because a high overall pass rate with one critical finding (like a data leak) can still be a launch blocker
Because severity levels are assigned randomly and don't matter
Because only low-severity findings are worth fixing
questions.explain: The lesson states that a 95% pass rate with one critical finding is still a launch blocker, so severity should guide prioritization over the aggregate number.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend doing once a red-team finding is identified and fixed?
options: Immediately forgetting about it since it's been fixed
Deleting all record that the finding ever existed
Adding the probe that found it to the regular eval dataset so a future change can't silently reopen it
Running the red-team tool only one more time and then stopping forever
questions.explain: The lesson recommends feeding fixed red-team findings back into the eval dataset so future changes are checked against them automatically.
